page: Amazon Web Services r4.4xlarge is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance running on the Xen hypervisor. It is powered by a 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 processor built on the x86_64 architecture, providing 16 dedicated virtual CPUs across 8 physical cores with multithreading enabled. The instance includes 122.0 GB of system memory, yielding approximately 7.62 GB of RAM per vCPU. Hardware acceleration is absent, with zero GPUs provisioned. The configuration contains no bundled local storage, relying on external network-attached volumes for disk access, and provides a 5 Gbps baseline network bandwidth.

Benchmark results highlight a divergence between single-threaded and parallel processing capabilities. Single-core evaluations place the older Broadwell architecture in lower tiers, demonstrated by a stress-ng score of 884.59 and a Geekbench single-core score of 907.0. Conversely, multithreaded benchmarks perform within median expectations, evidenced by a PassMark CPU score of 11526.34 and a multi-core Geekbench score of 5521.0. Uncached memory read bandwidth reaches 58.1 GB/sec, while uncached write bandwidth settles at 24.63 GB/sec. In-memory data throughput tests show 4.6 million Redis SET operations per second alongside steady throughput across standard static web serving benchmarks.

From an efficiency perspective, the r4.4xlarge offers high memory capacity at the expense of per-core compute performance and modern instruction set support, lacking AVX-512 extensions. The absence of integrated NVMe storage also shifts all I/O demands onto network-attached block devices. Consequently, this instance fits memory-heavy workloads that do not demand cutting-edge single-thread clock rates, such as mid-sized in-memory databases, distributed caching layers, enterprise application runtimes, and batch memory transformations.
description: Amazon Web Services r4.4xlarge is a memory-optimized instance tailored for workloads requiring significant memory capacity per vCPU. Driven by a 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 processor, it provisions 16 virtual CPUs over 8 physical cores alongside 122.0 GB of system RAM. The instance lacks local instance storage and dedicated GPU acceleration, relying on network-attached storage and offering a 5 Gbps baseline network bandwidth. Empirical benchmark testing reveals moderate multi-core throughput alongside modest single-core execution speeds typical of its CPU generation. Memory read bandwidth reaches 58.1 GB/sec for uncached blocks, supporting concurrent operations across its 16 vCPUs. Without local disks or advanced AVX-512 extensions, this instance offers a resource balance geared specifically toward memory-bound tasks. It is technically suitable for in-memory caching platforms, enterprise relational databases, medium-scale data analysis, and memory-intensive background processing jobs.
